record.title: TasteVal reports a 2.30× experimental-compute multiplier for Opus 5.5 on eight bounded AI R&D tasks
record.summary: Jaffe and Sherburn introduce TasteVal, an author-built benchmark of eight text and vision tasks intended to measure experimental design and interpretation when a fixed research problem is given. They report that Opus 5.5 (max) reaches a 2.30× experimental-compute multiplier against the best expert attempt per task (95% CI 1.15–4.37). The authors also estimate that frontier-model multiplier performance doubled about every 3.0 months after December 2025, while final normalized performance shows no corresponding trend break. These are preprint results on withheld tasks, not evidence that models choose valuable research questions or outperform experts across broad research work.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_PUBLICATION_EVENT
claims.text: The authors posted the TasteVal preprint, describing an evaluation of experimental research behavior on eight author-built tasks.

claims.label: CLAIMED_BY_AUTHORS
claims.text: The authors report that Opus 5.5 (max) achieved a 2.30× experimental-compute multiplier against the task-level best expert attempt (95% CI 1.15–4.37).

claims.label: CLAIMED_BY_AUTHORS
claims.text: The authors report that the compute multiplier for frontier models doubled about every 3.0 months after December 2025 (95% CI 1.7–5.0), while final normalized performance doubled every 14.6 months without a significant trend break.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_SCOPE_LIMIT
claims.text: The paper defines its measured construct as iterative experimental design and interpretation for a fixed problem; it does not measure problem selection or broad autonomous research.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or external assessment of the reported multiplier was identified in this activation.

The eight benchmark tasks are withheld to reduce contamination, preventing direct replication of the identical task set; task-level raw outcomes and a public executable artifact were not inspected in this activation.
The best expert attempt per task and chained compute-multiplier references may affect the estimate; no independent baseline audit was performed here.

brief.importance_rationale: If AI systems reliably use experimental compute more efficiently than strong human researchers, this could alter AI R&D throughput and resource planning. The reported 2.30× result is limited to eight author-built tasks and one evaluation setup, so field-wide consequences remain conditional.
limitations: The results are author-reported in one preprint and have not been independently reproduced.
Eight deliberately uncontaminated tasks are author-built; the authors withhold task content.
TasteVal isolates experiment design and interpretation for fixed research problems, not valuable problem selection, novel ideas or complete autonomous research.
The abstract's reported 2.30× multiplier compares with the best recruited expert attempt per task and does not establish broad superiority over human research teams or at equal dollar cost.

The reported $282 versus $9,123 per-run costs use author-selected API, GPU and salary assumptions; they do not show performance at equal dollar cost. The AI-R&D forecast scenarios are explicitly naive extrapolations that assume rate transfer from TasteVal to broader frontier work.

The authors also estimate that frontier-model multiplier performance doubled about every 3.0 months after December 2025, while final normalized performance shows no corresponding trend break. technical.claimed_result: The authors report a 2.30× experimental-compute multiplier for Opus 5.5 (max), with 95% CI 1.15–4.37, and a post-December-2025 trend in frontier-model multiplier doubling about every 3.0 months.
technical.compute_or_cost: The authors report an average $282 per Opus 5.5 run (API spend across agents plus GPU at $2.5/hour) versus $9,123 per expert baseline run, including salary at $119/hour—roughly 1/30 of the expert run cost. This is not a matched-dollar performance comparison. The 2.30× benchmark metric is serial experimental compute; forecast extrapolations assume, without established transfer, that the measured rate applies to broader frontier AI R&D.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint and its stated benchmark protocol are publicly available; the reported performance results remain author claims.
technical.implementation_status: Research benchmark preprint; no operational deployment effect established.
technical.mechanism: A Researcher model iteratively proposes experiments while a fixed Coder implements them and returns results; performance is expressed as a serial experimental-compute multiplier against recruited human experts.
technical.novelty: A benchmark focused on iterative experimental design and interpretation for fixed AI R&D tasks; transfer beyond the selected task construct remains unresolved.
technical.regime: Eight author-built text/vision tasks, 20 evaluated models, six seeds per model/task, up to 40 serial H100-hours or 120 wall-clock hours; task content withheld. These details are from the paper's reported protocol.
technical.reproducibility: No independent reproduction. The task set is withheld; full protocol details and analysis are described in the preprint.
technical.strongest_baseline: Best recruited human expert attempt on each of eight tasks, as defined by the authors. No external audit of this baseline was performed.

brief.title: TasteVal reports a 2.30× experimental-compute multiplier for Opus 5.5 on eight bounded AI R&D tasks
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported efficiency gain transfers to larger and less scripted research settings, it could reduce compute per experimental result and change research-program planning. The benchmark measures iterative experiment design for fixed problems; it does not measure problem selection, novel idea generation, open-ended project execution, or real-time multi-agent research.
